topic.name: Architecture & Multi-Tenant SaaS
topic.tagline: Boundaries, tenancy, billing, audits, and systems that stay sane.
topic.description: Go beyond a single CRUD screen. Learn where business logic belongs, how to isolate tenants, how to design billing and audit flows, and which trade-offs matter when the app becomes a product with real operational and legal obligations.

questions.prompt: Where should the logic for 'place an order' live?
choices: Entirely inside the view, including payment calls and emails.
In a focused service/domain function or method that the view calls, with the view handling HTTP concerns.
questions.explanation: Views should parse HTTP input, enforce access, call application logic, and shape a response. A service function can coordinate validation, transactions, stock, payment, and events, and can be reused by the admin, API, and tasks.

questions.prompt: Why define AUTH_USER_MODEL and a custom user model at the start of a project?
choices: Changing the user model after migrations and foreign keys exist is a painful, risky migration.
Django requires a custom user model to run.
It removes the need for authentication.
questions.explanation: Even if the default User fits today, a custom subclass (or a model with a UUID/email login) gives room to grow. Set AUTH_USER_MODEL before the first migration. Retrofitting later touches many tables and third-party apps.

questions.prompt: Where should production secrets such as database passwords and API keys live?
choices: Committed in settings.py so every environment is identical.
In environment variables or a secrets manager, injected at deploy time and never committed.
In the database as plain text.
questions.explanation: Settings should read secrets from the environment or a secret manager. Keep a safe .env.example with names only. Rotate exposed keys, restrict access, and ensure debug pages/logs do not print secrets.

questions.prompt: What is an audit log for?
choices: Recording who changed sensitive data or performed privileged actions, when, and from where.
questions.explanation: An audit trail supports security investigations, compliance, and customer support. Record actor, action, target, before/after where appropriate, timestamp, and request context. Treat it as append-only and protect it from normal app edits.

questions.prompt: What is a feature flag useful for?
choices: Turning a feature on or off for selected users, tenants, or a percentage without redeploying.
questions.explanation: Feature flags separate deployment from release and support gradual rollouts, beta access, and fast rollback. They add state and cleanup work. Do not use flags as a substitute for authorization or delete them once fully rolled out.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off between shared-schema tenancy and schema-per-tenant?
choices: Shared schema is simpler and cheaper but requires rigorous tenant scoping; schema-per-tenant isolates data but multiplies migrations and connections.
Schema-per-tenant is always faster for every query.
Shared schema automatically prevents cross-tenant leaks.
questions.explanation: Shared schema with tenant_id is operationally simple and common. Schema-per-tenant provides stronger isolation but complicates migrations, backups, routing, and connection pools. Database-per-tenant goes further with more cost. Choose based on isolation, scale, and ops capacity.

questions.prompt: A view uses Invoice.objects.get(pk=request.POST["invoice_id"]). What is missing?
choices: A query scoped to the requesting user/tenant so an ID from another account cannot be fetched.
questions.explanation: Never trust an object ID from the client. Use get_object_or_404(Invoice, pk=..., tenant=request.tenant) or a scoped manager. ID enumeration is one of the most common cross-tenant leaks. Add object-level permissions for the action too.

questions.prompt: What should a billing webhook endpoint verify before changing a subscription?
choices: The provider signature, the event type/version, and an idempotent event record; then reconcile against server-side state.
The request came from the same IP forever.
questions.explanation: Verify the raw-body signature with the provider secret, reject stale/replayed events, deduplicate by event ID, and make state transitions idempotent. Do not trust customer-supplied plan or price IDs; map them to server-side records.

questions.prompt: What context should a background job carry in a multi-tenant system?
choices: Nothing; it can discover the tenant later.
The tenant identifier and the minimal entity IDs needed, with the worker re-establishing tenant-scoped access.
A copy of every tenant's database.
questions.explanation: Tasks must not rely on an ambient request context. Carry tenant_id and entity IDs explicitly, re-fetch data, and enforce scoping in the worker. Prevent jobs from one tenant reading another's rows; add tests that switch tenant context.

choices: One deployment with explicit internal modules/boundaries, shared infrastructure, and disciplined interfaces between domains.
A monolith where every module imports every other module.
questions.explanation: A modular monolith keeps deployment simple while drawing boundaries around billing, accounts, catalog, and other domains. Modules communicate through services/events rather than reaching into each other's tables. You can extract a module later if scale demands it.

questions.prompt: Which additional control most reduces the risk of a cross-tenant data leak?
choices: Defence in depth: scoped querysets/managers, tenant-aware permissions, database constraints, tests, and optional row-level security.
questions.explanation: One scoped query is not enough. Use a tenant-aware data-access layer, object permissions, unique constraints including tenant_id, automated isolation tests, and Postgres row-level security where appropriate. Log and alert on unusual cross-tenant access attempts.

questions.prompt: Why is a database transaction not enough to guarantee a billing state change plus an external event?
choices: The external system is outside the transaction and can succeed while the database rolls back, or vice versa.
Billing providers do not use HTTP.
questions.explanation: You cannot atomically commit a local transaction and an external API call. Use idempotency keys, an outbox, provider reconciliation, and a state machine with clear pending/succeeded/failed states. Never assume a 200 response means the whole workflow is consistent.

questions.prompt: A customer requests deletion under privacy rules. What is the most complete approach?
choices: Delete the User row and assume all data is gone.
Inventory personal data, delete or anonymise records across services, handle backups/retention and audit obligations, and record the request.
Disable the customer's login and keep everything.
questions.explanation: Deletion is a cross-cutting data-governance workflow: discover copies, handle relational references, anonymise where deletion conflicts with legal retention, expire backups according to policy, and verify. Keep a minimal audit record of the request without retaining the deleted content.

questions.prompt: What is the key risk of sending reads to a replica immediately after a write?
choices: Replication lag can return stale data or a missing row.
questions.explanation: Replication is usually asynchronous. A read-after-write workflow may need to stick to the primary for a short window, use a consistent-read token, or route the specific query to the writer. Design UX for eventual consistency where it is acceptable.

questions.prompt: One tenant starts a huge export and slows everyone down. What is the best response?
choices: Use per-tenant quotas, rate limits, fair queues, and background exports with throttling and status reporting.
questions.explanation: Noisy-neighbour control is an architectural requirement. Apply per-tenant quotas and concurrency limits, separate heavy jobs from interactive traffic, stream or chunk large exports, and surface progress. Protect shared resources before a customer discovers the limit for you.

flashcards.front: Where should business logic live in a Django app?
flashcards.back: Not spread across fat views, templates, and model save overrides. Put meaningful workflows in services/domain functions with explicit inputs, transactions, and side effects. Views handle HTTP; models own data invariants; tasks call the same services.

flashcards.front: Why start with a custom user model?
flashcards.back: It gives you room to change identifiers, add fields, or use email login without a brutal migration later. Set AUTH_USER_MODEL before the first migration. Do not overbuild it; a simple subclass is enough to start.

Shared schema with tenant_id is simpler and cheaper but demands rigorous scoping. Schema-per-tenant offers stronger isolation with heavier migrations, connections, and ops. Database-per-tenant isolates further at higher cost. Choose based on isolation and operational capacity.

flashcards.front: How do you prevent IDOR/cross-tenant access?
flashcards.back: Scope every query by the authenticated user/tenant, check object permissions, validate foreign-key ownership, and add tests that attempt cross-tenant access. Never rely on unguessable IDs. Use 404 for resources the caller should not know exist.

flashcards.front: How do you keep billing state correct across webhooks and your database?
flashcards.back: Verify signatures, deduplicate event IDs, store a state machine, use idempotency keys, and reconcile against the provider. Use an outbox for outbound events. Treat webhook delivery as at-least-once and never trust client-supplied plan/price data.

flashcards.front: What belongs in an audit log?
flashcards.back: Actor, action, target, timestamp, source/request context, and relevant before/after values for sensitive changes. Protect it as append-only, redact secrets, define retention, and make it queryable for investigations. Do not turn it into a second mutable business table.
flashcards.hint: Who did what to what, when.

flashcards.front: Why plan for noisy neighbours in a SaaS?
flashcards.back: One tenant's export, webhook flood, or expensive query can starve everyone. Apply per-tenant quotas, concurrency/rate limits, fair queues, query timeouts, and separate heavy jobs from interactive traffic. Measure per-tenant cost and enforce it.
